---
title: "Quiz: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Numbers use green light, λ = 520 nm.

---

**Q1.** Two points are 0.61λ/NA apart. What does the profile through them look like? And at 0.47λ/NA?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Rayleigh and Sparrow.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At 0.61λ/NA (Rayleigh) the peak of each point lies on the first dark ring of the other: two peaks with a dip of about 26 % between them. At 0.47λ/NA (Sparrow) the dip has just vanished: the profile is flat at the midpoint, a single broad peak.
:::

---

**Q2.** Two molecules are exactly at the Rayleigh distance, but each delivers only 20 photons. Are they resolved?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many photons land in the brightest pixel, and how large is the Poisson noise there?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
In practice no. With 65 nm pixels about 9 % of a point's photons land in its peak pixel: about 2 photons, with noise $\pm\sqrt2 \approx \pm 1.4$, i.e. ±70 %. A 26 % dip is far below that noise. The Rayleigh criterion assumes a noise-free image; with few photons, noise decides what can be resolved.
:::

---

**Q3.** A 60× / 1.4 oil objective is used with a camera of 6.5 µm pixels. Is the image Nyquist sampled at 520 nm?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Pixel in the sample plane = camera pixel ÷ magnification; Nyquist = λ/4NA.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pixel in the sample: $6500/60 = 108$ nm. Nyquist: $520/(4 \cdot 1.4) = 93$ nm. Slightly undersampled (by 1.17×): the finest detail the lens passes, near the cut-off, can alias. A 1.5× extra magnifier (72 nm) would fix it.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why not simply use pixels much smaller than Nyquist, to be safe?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the number of photons per pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The optics deliver no detail beyond the cut-off, so smaller pixels add none. But the same photons are spread over more pixels: each pixel is noisier (shot noise relative to the signal grows, and every pixel adds its own read noise). Files grow and acquisitions slow down; for live samples, more light per useful pixel means more bleaching.
:::

---

**Q5.** A widefield z-stack is taken with an NA 1.4 objective and 1 µm steps. What goes wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Axial Nyquist at NA 1.4 is about 280 nm; the PSF is about 0.5 µm long (FWHM).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The z-step is about 3.6 times too large. A small object halfway between two planes (0.5 µm from each) appears in neither at full brightness: on the axis the PSF has dropped to about 4 % of its peak there. Axial detail is aliased or lost, and deconvolution cannot recover it afterwards.
:::

---

**Q6.** What is the "missing cone" of a widefield microscope, and what does it mean for the image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where in 3D frequency space is the widefield OTF zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The 3D OTF of a widefield microscope is zero in a cone around the $k_z$ axis: structures that vary slowly sideways but change along $z$ (a uniform layer, a large flat sheet) are not transmitted in their $z$-variation. In the image, out-of-focus light from such structures is spread over neighbouring planes, not removed: widefield has no optical sectioning. A confocal pinhole fills the cone.
:::

---

**Q7.** You measure a PSF with 200 nm beads and get an FWHM of 230 nm. Is the PSF really that wide?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\text{FWHM}_\text{meas}^2 \approx \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + (0.53D)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No: the bead itself adds about $0.53 \cdot 200 = 105$ nm in quadrature. $\sqrt{230^2 - 105^2} \approx 204$ nm. Use smaller beads (100 nm or less) so that the correction is small.
:::

---

**Q8.** Why average many beads instead of measuring one very carefully?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to independent noise when you average $N$ copies?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each bead's image is noisy; after background subtraction and sub-pixel centring, averaging $N$ of them keeps the PSF and reduces the noise by $\sqrt N$ (30 beads: to 18 %). A single bead can only be made less noisy with more photons, which bleaches it.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Show that for a Gaussian PSF with standard deviation σ, two equal points are just at the Sparrow limit when they are 2σ apart.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The midpoint curvature of $h(x - d/2) + h(x + d/2)$ is $2h''(d/2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$h(x) = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}$ has $h''(x) = (x^2/\sigma^4 - 1/\sigma^2)\,h(x)$, zero at $x = \sigma$. The midpoint curvature $2h''(d/2)$ changes sign at $d/2 = \sigma$: below $d = 2\sigma$ the midpoint is a maximum (one peak), above it a minimum (a dip).
:::
